## Theme 1 — Pain & Occasion / Schmerz & Anlass

> **Why this block:** Every platform intervention begins with a presenting problem that may or may not be the real problem. This block surfaces who names the pain, what triggered the review now, and what inaction actually costs — separating the real driver from the stated one before any technical assessment begins.

> **Red flags:**
> - Pain described only from one stakeholder group, not cross-checked with consumers or operators.
> - No one has tried to fix this before — or no one knows whether it was tried.
> - Trigger is an external deadline; underlying operational situation is stable or unknown.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - No clear pain owner and no mandate to define one → stop; clarify mandate first.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Presenting pain is a symptom, not a root cause* — scope: When pain is described exclusively from one stakeholder perspective and no attempt to cross-check has been made. Falsifiable by: A single documented technical or organisational event that is the traceable cause.
> - *The trigger is external, the pain is internal* — scope: When the review is precipitated by an audit, contract renewal, or regulatory deadline rather than operational failure. Falsifiable by: A documented operational metric that was already deteriorating before the external trigger.

## Theme 2 — Success & Benchmark / Erfolg & Messlatte

> **Why this block:** A platform decision without a measurable success criterion is a preference, not a decision. This block captures the Entscheidungskopf — the decision question, its owner, its explicit scope boundary, and its deadline — alongside the criteria by which any outcome will be judged.

> **Red flags:**
> - No named decision owner — "the architecture board" or "leadership" is not an owner.
> - Success is defined only in terms of what is built, not in terms of outcomes.
> - Deadline is stated but its consequence if missed is unknown or "not yet defined".

> **Stop conditions:**
> - No decision question can be formulated → stop; the intake is premature.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Success criteria are stated but not measurable* — scope: When the stated success is expressed in qualitative terms ("better", "faster") with no observable indicator. Falsifiable by: A named metric with a target value and a measurement method.
> - *The deadline is political, not operational* — scope: When the deadline aligns with a budget cycle, a personnel change, or an external milestone rather than a technical dependency. Falsifiable by: A documented technical dependency that establishes the deadline independently.

## Theme 3 — Constraints & Phase / Vorgaben & Phase

> **Why this block:** Fixed constraints collapse the option space before analysis begins. Discovering a hard mandate late — a vendor lock-in, a budget ceiling, a regulatory timeline — invalidates work already done. This block captures what cannot be changed.

> **Red flags:**
> - Budget stated as "TBD" for a decision with a firm deadline.
> - Mandate attributed to a person rather than a policy or contract.
> - Governance process timeline is unknown but the decision deadline is fixed.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - None specific; flag for Discovery if regulatory timelines are unknown — Q3.4 is no_defaults: leave blank, mark to-verify.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Stated mandates are softer than they appear* — scope: When constraints are stated as "we use X" rather than "we must use X per signed contract / policy reference N". Falsifiable by: A signed contract clause or a named policy document with the exact requirement.

## Theme 4 — Inventory & Knowledge / Bestand & Wissen

> **Why this block:** Brownfield platforms accumulate components that no one fully understands. Dark zones — parts of the system whose behaviour is known only through observation, not documentation — are the primary source of architectural surprise. This block maps what exists and who knows it.

> **Red flags:**
> - Only one person understands a critical path component.
> - No automated test suite — changes are verified manually or in production.
> - Master data exists in more than one system with no documented reconciliation process.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If the dark zone covers a component involved in any proposed migration path → flag as a pre-condition for Discovery work, not a Discovery finding.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *The dark zone is concentrated, not distributed* — scope: When the least-understood component is a legacy module written by a single person or team that has since left. Falsifiable by: Multiple team members who can independently describe the component's behaviour with matching accounts.
> - *Documentation describes the intended system, not the running one* — scope: Systems older than 3 years with no documented verification process. Falsifiable by: A documented audit comparing specification against observed runtime behaviour within the last 12 months.

## Theme 5 — Consumers & Interfaces / Konsumenten & Schnittstellen

> **Why this block:** A platform migration that breaks a consumer is not a platform migration — it is an incident. This block maps who depends on what, which dependencies are formally contracted versus informally assumed, and who has the authority to accept a breaking change.

> **Red flags:**
> - Shadow integrations exist that the platform team did not know about.
> - No one can identify who would approve a breaking change for a given consumer.
> - SLA commitments are verbal or email-based, not in a signed document.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If no consumer inventory exists → treat as a pre-condition for any migration option, not as a Design input.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Informal consumers will surface only when broken* — scope: Platforms older than 3 years in organisations where interface usage is not instrumented or logged. Falsifiable by: Complete API access logs showing all callers over a 90-day window.
> - *The most critical consumer is not the most vocal one* — scope: When requirements gathering was driven by the loudest team rather than by dependency graph analysis. Falsifiable by: A dependency map that ranks consumers by data-flow criticality rather than relationship.

## Theme 6 — Data & Sovereignty / Daten & Souveränität

> **Why this block:** Data classification determines which options are legally available. Missing retention schedules and erasure paths are not implementation details — they are blocking constraints that invalidate entire migration options. This block surfaces the data layer before options are evaluated.

> **Red flags:**
> - Data classification is "TBD" or "same as source system" with no documented review.
> - No named data owner for any domain.
> - Retention requirements are unknown — this is a no_defaults field; leave blank, flag to-verify.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If Q6.1, Q6.2 and Q6.4 are all unknown → stop migration options analysis; the data posture must be established before options can be evaluated.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Classification was inherited from the source system, not assessed for the platform* — scope: Migrations where data from multiple source systems is combined in a new context. Falsifiable by: A documented classification review that evaluated the aggregated dataset rather than each source in isolation.
> - *The erasure path exists on paper but not in practice* — scope: All platforms that have never received an erasure request. Falsifiable by: A logged, tested end-to-end erasure showing removal across all storage layers.

**Mini data inventory** — one row per data domain:

| Domain | Classification | Owner | Retention | Erasure Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | |

## Theme 7 — Regulation & Trust / Regulatorik & Vertrauen

> **Why this block:** Regulatory obligations are not architectural inputs — they are constraints that determine which options are available at all. The AI scoping question is a scoping decision, not a checklist. This block surfaces what applies, what is uncertain, and what Legal has said.

> **Red flags:**
> - AI risk class is stated without a named Legal opinion.
> - Open audit findings are unresolved — their status must be known before options analysis.
> - Regulatory framework was last reviewed more than 2 years ago.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If Q7.1 is unknown and the platform touches personal data → stop; the regulatory posture must be clarified before migration options can be evaluated.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Regulatory applicability was assumed, not assessed* — scope: When regulatory statements are attributed to convention ("we're always regulated like this") rather than a named legal opinion or compliance review with a date. Falsifiable by: A documented regulatory applicability assessment with a named assessor and date.

## Theme 8 — Migration & Reversibility / Migration & Reversibilität

> **Why this block:** Every migration path has at least one step from which return is difficult or impossible. "Return is impossible" is a valid, documentable answer — pretending otherwise creates options that do not exist. This block forces irreversibility to be named explicitly.

> **Red flags:**
> - Irreversible steps are listed as "risks" rather than as named, dated decision points.
> - Rollback is described as possible but has never been rehearsed.
> - Historical data migration is deferred to "phase 2" with no defined phase 2.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If Q8.2 is answered and the irreversible step is the first one → options must explicitly include "defer decision and complete Discovery" before the irreversible step is sanctioned.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *The dual-write window is underestimated* — scope: Migrations involving master data with many consumers and no single transactional authority. Falsifiable by: A documented load test or proof-of-concept that measured actual synchronisation latency under production-like conditions.
> - *Cutover is treated as a technical event, not a business continuity event* — scope: When the cutover plan is owned by engineering with no explicit sign-off from operations or the business. Falsifiable by: A cutover plan that names a business-side go/no-go authority and defines rollback trigger criteria in business terms.

## Theme 9 — Organisation & Team / Organisation & Team-Schnitt

> **Why this block:** Platform decisions are also team decisions. The way work is structured, where knowledge lives, and who talks to whom determine what is achievable — and on what timeline. This block surfaces the organisational reality before any delivery estimate is formed.

> **Red flags:**
> - Only one person understands the deployment pipeline or the production data model.
> - Key knowledge holders have announced departure or have recently left.
> - The platform team is below minimum viable size for the maintenance burden they carry.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If Q9.3 reveals that the sole knowledge holder is leaving within the migration window → flag as a pre-condition; knowledge transfer becomes a phase-zero activity.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *The formal owner and the effective owner are different people* — scope: Platforms handed over without a full knowledge transfer, or "inherited" by a team that did not build them. Falsifiable by: The formal owner can independently answer Q4.3 without consulting the person who actually knows.
> - *Cognitive load of the platform team blocks the migration, not technical complexity* — scope: Teams that maintain multiple legacy platforms simultaneously. Falsifiable by: Team capacity analysis showing available bandwidth against the migration effort estimate.
> - *Informal veto power sits outside the formal decision chain* — scope: Organisations where platform decisions have previously been reversed after formal approval. Falsifiable by: A mapping of all previous reversals against the people involved.

## Theme 10 — Operations, Security & Resilience / Betrieb, Sicherheit & Resilienz

> **Why this block:** A platform that cannot describe its own operational posture cannot safely migrate. This block captures the minimum operational and security facts that any migration option depends on. If all of Q10.1, Q10.2, Q10.5 and Q10.6 are unknown, the stop condition applies.

> **Red flags:**
> - No SLO exists — this is a no_defaults field; state "none defined", do not estimate.
> - Restore has never been tested — RTO/RPO targets are theoretical.
> - Production access is not inventoried or reviewed regularly.
> - Encryption at rest or in transit is unknown — leave blank, flag as to-verify.

> **Stop conditions:**
> - If Q10.1, Q10.2, Q10.5 and Q10.6 are all unknown or blank → stop; the operational blind spot must be resolved before any migration option can be evaluated. Document this stop condition in the To-Verify register.

> **Patterns & hypotheses — not questions:**
> - *Operational posture was sufficient for the current system but will not transfer* — scope: Migrations that move from a self-managed on-premise system to a managed cloud service, or vice versa, where observability and access control models differ fundamentally. Falsifiable by: A documented mapping of current operational controls to the target environment.
